senses: A scientist specializing in understanding and describing the nature of the universe.
The film (movie) industry; the people who work in that industry.
A Philippine television drama, serialized in the manner of a soap opera.
One of the cabalistic aspects of the soul, related to emotion and morality.
A little wing.
The bastard wing or alula of a bird.
The pterygium of a weevil.
Resembling a stylus or pen.
ety: From style or stylus + -oid (“-like, resembling”). Compare Ancient Greek στῡλοειδής (stūloeidḗs).

senses: A small water-repelling, cone-shaped projection used in the architrave of the Doric order in classical architecture.
A small round spot of colour.
ety: From Middle English gutta, from Latin gutta. Doublet of gout and goutte.

senses: Belonging or pertaining to the group Eutheria, comprising the mammals more closely related to animals like humans and rodents than to marsupials.
ety: From Eutheria, from Ancient Greek εὖ (eû, “good, true”) + θηρίον (thēríon, “beast”).

senses: A female prosecutor
A female victim of a crime on whose behalf the state is prosecuting a suspect
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin prōsecūtrīx. By surface analysis, prosecutor + -trix.
examples: A man, in the desperation of a refusal (common people take those things strangely to heart), had stabbed the obdurate fair one with his knife. She was herself the prosecutrix.

The paper reports today that Inger Marie Sunde, a prosecutrix in charge of what the locals call Okokrim (white collar crime), put young Jon on the stand again and probed for inconsistencies in his answers.

senses: A body of people considered as a whole.
Synonym of sexy
ety: Representing pronunciation of sexy with a prolonged final syllable; compare partay.

senses: Jade, nephrite.
examples: Over time, the hooks became increasingly stylized and now are a popular shape for decorative pounamu pendants called hei matau, the first word indicating that the matau is worn around the neck.

senses: A samurai's armor for the arms, thighs, and shins.
An administrative unit in South Korea, corresponding to a small rural township.
A person who patches something.
The driver's assistant or lackey in a team of miners.
A person, especially a philosopher, who studies ethics (principles governing right and wrong conduct).
A person who advocates a particular set of principles governing right and wrong conduct.
ety: From ethics + -ist, changing /ks/ to /θ/ for ease of pronunciation and dropping the -s.

senses: A dumpling in Korean cuisine.
ety: Borrowed from Korean 만두(饅頭) (mandu), in turn from Chinese 饅頭 /馒头 (mántou). Doublet of manju, manti, and mantou.
examples: Mandu are the traditional fast food of the region and make a great meal or snack for the road.
Preheat the oil to 350°F (180°C) and fry the mandu in batches until golden and crispy.
When you have made all the mandu, heat about a tablespoon of groundnut oil in a non-stick frying pan or a wok that has a lid.

senses: A group of microorganisms only differing from others by their composition in terms of antigens
A container, generally of plastic, which is not a simple tube and which is kept with its cap down.
Having a regular rhythm.
ety: From New Latin metricus + -al. For sense 4: Compare Russian метри́ческий (metríčeskij).

senses: Someone who studies lepidoptery; someone who studies butterflies and moths.
The emir of a Hausa-Fulani emirate.
Having chambers.
A schoolchild, a kid who attends school; a schoolboy or schoolgirl.
In Carnatic music, a type of short song, or the accompanying dance.

senses: A long object, often a timber or log, buried to serve as an anchor for a wall or for stays.
A cutout device that operates in the event that an operator releases the control handles, leaves the operator's seat, or otherwise seems to be no longer present and alert.
ety: From dead + man. In the sense referring to a safety switch, the notion of an operator who is dead is the figurative archetype representing any incapacitation, absence, or inattention. See also Dead Hand in that regard.
examples: The building code requires deadmen for retaining walls.

senses: A medical device similar to the outer ring of a contraceptive diaphragm, most commonly used to support a displaced uterus; also called therapeutic pessary.
A diaphragm or cervical cap.
ety: From Middle English pessarie, from Old French pessaire, from Latin pessarium.

senses: A double ikat, usually silk, from Gujarat, western India.
Luffa spp. (Philippine usage).
Trichosanthes cucumerina (Sinhalese usage).
Trichosanthes dioica (Portuguese usage).
ety: Borrowed from Gujarati પટોળાં (paṭoḷā̃), plural of પટોળું (paṭoḷũ).

senses: A gladiatorial training school.
A private school for teaching children reading, writing, arithmetic, and sometimes Greek.
The branch of theology concerned with the doctrines, role etc. of a church.
The science of building and decorating churches.
ety: From ecclesio- + -logy. Coined by a writer of the British Critic in 1837, as ecclesialogy.

senses: The residue from processing sugar cane or other plants such as sorghum or sugar beet after the juice is extracted.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French bagasse, from Spanish bagazo (“plant residue (especially from sugar cane) after juice is extracted”), from baga (“berry”) (from Latin bāca (“berry or other small fruit; etc.”); further etymology uncertain) + -azo (augmentative suffix).

senses: Nerdy; bookish; having the qualities of a wonk.
examples: According to Greer, the voting classes were ready for someone very much like the wonkish Clinton, with his devotion to "the issues."
Hillary may have been too wonkish, and Palin not wonkish enough, but they have normalized white females as political candidates for the nation.
Being a renegade Islamo-punk had run its course, but now I answered brothers' questions in a wonkish intellectual way, ducking and weaving around the truth claims.

senses: The quality or extent of being controllable; controllableness.
examples: These conditions are discussed under the subjects of controllability, stabilizability, reconstructability, and detectability in the literature on linear optimal control.

A freshwater mussel, usually edible, of the order Unionida in subclass Palaeoheterodonta.
Any of certain other bivalves of somewhat similar appearance, such as the zebra mussel and quagga mussel of the family Dreissenidae in subclass Heterodonta.
ety: From Middle English muscle (“mussel”), from Old English muscle, from Proto-West Germanic *muskulā, from Late Latin muscula, from Latin mūsculus (“mussel, muscle”, literally “little mouse”). Doublet of muscle.

senses: One who saws; a sawyer.

senses: An obsolete currency in Curaçao, equivalent to six stuivers.
ety: From Dutch reaal, from Spanish real. Doublet of royal.

The pin at the centre of the triangle of bowling pins (originally the tallest pin in kayles). Sometimes also the headpin at the apex.
The bolt holding together the truck of a roller skate or skateboard.
Like a scar, or rocky eminence.

senses: A process of force-feeding a goose for foie gras
A process of force-feeding cattle for veal
ety: Borrowed from French gavage, from gaver (“to stuff or cram”).

A wild horse.
